terms.short: The third form of a verb — the one used after have or be. Go, went, gone: gone is the past participle.
terms.example: I have seen it. (see → saw → seen)

terms.short: The plain past form, used for something finished at a known time in the past.
terms.example: We went to the coast last summer.

terms.short: The everyday present form, used for habits and facts. Add -s for he, she and it.
terms.example: She works in a bakery.

terms.short: have or has plus the past participle. Used when a past action still matters now, or the period is unfinished.
terms.example: I have lived here since 2019.

terms.short: had plus the past participle. Used for the earlier of two past events.
terms.example: She had left before I arrived.

terms.short: The form of a verb that shows when something happens — past, present or future.
terms.example: eats (present) → ate (past)

terms.short: The basic form of a verb, usually with to in front of it.
terms.example: She wants to leave.

terms.short: The verb with -ing on the end. Some verbs must be followed by it instead of the infinitive.
terms.example: He denied knowing about it.

terms.short: A helping verb — be, have or do — that goes in front of the main verb to build a tense, a question or a negative.
terms.example: Did you see it? (did is the auxiliary)

terms.short: Swapping the subject and the auxiliary, so the verb comes first. English does this after a negative word at the start of a sentence.
terms.example: Rarely have we seen this.

terms.short: When a word is moved to the very start of a sentence for emphasis. In English this often forces inversion.
terms.example: Seldom does he complain.

terms.short: The person or thing doing the action in a sentence.
terms.example: The dog barked. (the dog is the subject)

terms.short: The person or thing the action happens to.
terms.example: She read the book. (the book is the object)

terms.short: A word for a person, place or thing.
terms.example: teacher, city, water

terms.short: A word for an action or a state.
terms.example: run, think, be

terms.short: A word that describes a noun.
terms.example: a heavy box

terms.short: A word that describes a verb — how, when or how much. Many end in -ly.
terms.example: Prices rose sharply.

terms.short: The little words a, an and the that go before a noun.
terms.example: a bus, the bus

terms.short: A small word showing place, time or direction — in, on, at, since, for.
terms.example: on Monday, at six o'clock

terms.short: What kind of word it is — noun, verb, adjective, adverb and so on. Knowing which one a gap needs narrows the answer fast.
terms.example: risen sharply needs an adverb, not an adjective.

terms.short: Words that native speakers naturally put together. The grammar of an alternative may be fine and still sound wrong.
terms.example: make a decision, not do a decision

terms.short: A verb plus a small word that changes its meaning completely.
terms.example: call off means cancel

terms.short: A fixed expression whose meaning you cannot work out from the separate words.
terms.example: damn with faint praise

terms.short: How formal or informal language is. The same idea has a formal version and a casual one, and exams reward choosing the right one.
terms.example: corroborate (formal) vs back up (casual)

terms.short: Admitting a point that works against your argument, usually before making your real point. Watch for although, while and for all.
terms.example: Although it was expensive, she booked it.

terms.short: The -er or more form, used to compare two things.
terms.example: heavier, more careful

terms.short: The -est or most form, used for the top of a group of three or more.
terms.example: the heaviest box

terms.short: if plus the present simple, then will. Used for a real future possibility.
terms.example: If it rains, we'll cancel.

terms.short: if plus the past simple, then would. Used for something imagined or unlikely now.
terms.example: If I had time, I would come.

terms.short: if plus the past perfect, then would have. Used for a past that did not happen.
terms.example: If she had studied, she would have passed.

terms.short: When the thing having something done to it becomes the subject. Built with be plus the past participle.
terms.example: The report was finished on Friday.

terms.short: A part of a sentence starting with who, which, that or whose, adding information about a noun.
terms.example: The candidate, whose experience is limited, interviewed well.

terms.short: A part of a sentence with its own subject and verb.
terms.example: She left because it was late. (two clauses)

terms.short: The form that shows something belongs to someone — its, his, their, or 's.
terms.example: whatever its merits

terms.short: he, she, it, or one person or thing. In the present simple its verb takes an -s.
terms.example: My brother works here.

terms.short: A noun you cannot count one by one, so it has no plural and takes is, not are.
terms.example: water, money, advice

terms.short: More than one. Usually made by adding -s, and it takes are rather than is.
terms.example: There are two apples.

terms.short: A sentence with not, never or no in it. English uses any rather than some inside one.
terms.example: I don't have any money.

terms.short: Saying the same thing in different words. IELTS answers almost always paraphrase the passage rather than repeat it.
terms.example: distinct pattern → its own character

terms.short: A wrong option built to look right — usually real words from the text arranged into a claim the text never makes.
terms.example: A price that was mentioned, but not the one asked for.

terms.short: When a speaker says something and then changes it. In IELTS listening the second version is always the answer.
terms.example: Tuesday — sorry, make that Thursday.

terms.short: The passage says nothing about it either way. Choose this whenever you are arguing from what the writer would probably think.
terms.example: Two facts side by side are not a comparison.

terms.short: The passage states this, in these words or in different ones.
terms.example: Same meaning, different wording, still TRUE.

terms.short: The passage states the opposite. Not the same as saying nothing about it.
terms.example: Passage: lighter. Statement: heavier. That is FALSE.

terms.short: A word with almost the same meaning as another.
terms.example: cancel and call off

terms.short: A word that adds information to another word. Adjectives modify nouns; adverbs modify verbs.
terms.example: sharply modifies risen.

terms.short: A European scale of English levels, A1 (beginner) to C2 (near-native). Roughly: B1 is band 4–5, B2 is band 5.5–6.5, C1 is band 7–8.
terms.example: B2 is about band 6.

terms.short: The IELTS score, from 1 to 9, given in half steps. Most universities ask for 6.0 to 7.0.
terms.example: Band 6.5 overall.

terms.short: The words go together the way a native speaker would say them, even if other words would be grammatically correct.
terms.example: a flagrant breach, not a fiery breach

terms.short: Knowing what you do and do not know. Poor metacognition is why people feel sure of a wrong answer.
terms.example: Judging your own memory before trusting it.

terms.short: The recorded history of who has owned an object, from when it was made until now.
terms.example: A gap in the provenance is a problem.

terms.short: A study that follows the same people over a long period, rather than testing them once.
terms.example: A ten-year longitudinal study.

terms.short: Speaking at a natural speed without long pauses. It is about keeping going, not about speaking fast.
terms.example: Pausing to think is fine; pausing to hunt for a word is not.

terms.short: Whether your ideas follow one another in an order a listener can track. You can be fluent and still be hard to follow.
terms.example: Answer the question first, then give the reason.

terms.short: How wide and precise your vocabulary is. Examiners credit the right word more than the rare word.
terms.example: A sharp rise beats a big rise.

terms.short: How many different structures you use, and how correctly. Using only simple sentences caps this score even if nothing is wrong.
terms.example: Mix simple, compound and complex sentences.

terms.short: Whether your essay answers the whole question asked, with a clear position and enough support.
terms.example: Two parts in the question means two parts in the answer.

terms.short: In Task 1, whether you have reported the key information accurately and covered the main trends.
terms.example: Describe what the data shows, do not explain why.

terms.short: The words that join your ideas together — however, therefore, on the other hand. Too few is confusing; too many sounds mechanical.
terms.example: However, the figure fell again after 2015.

terms.short: Short words and phrases that signal what is coming next: a contrast, an example, a conclusion.
terms.example: For instance, in other words, as a result.

terms.short: The first sentence of a paragraph, saying what the paragraph is about. Examiners look for one in every body paragraph.
terms.example: The clearest benefit is cost.

terms.short: Softening a claim so it is not stronger than your evidence — may, tends to, in most cases.
terms.example: This may partly explain the fall.

terms.short: Telling the listener or reader where you are going before you go there.
terms.example: I will look at two reasons. The first is cost.

terms.short: Sounds and words used while thinking — um, er, like, you know. A few are natural; a lot break your fluency score.
terms.example: Replace um with a short silent pause.

terms.short: The verb must match its subject in number: one thing takes is, more than one takes are.
terms.example: The results are clear, not the results is clear.

terms.short: Using the right form of a word for its job in the sentence — succeed, success, successful, successfully.
terms.example: It was a successful trial, not a success trial.

terms.short: Two complete sentences joined with only a comma, or with nothing. Use a full stop, a semicolon, or a joining word.
terms.example: It rained, we stayed in. → It rained, so we stayed in.

terms.short: Rewriting the exam question in your own words to open an essay. Copying it word for word earns you nothing.
terms.example: Change the nouns and the sentence shape, not just one word.

terms.short: In Task 1, the sentence that states the biggest overall pattern. Leaving it out limits the band, however good the detail is.
terms.example: Overall, sales rose steadily throughout the period.

terms.short: The card in Part 2 of the speaking test giving a topic and four points. You get one minute to prepare and speak for up to two.
terms.example: Cover all four bullets and keep talking.
